authoritativeText.text:
一块石头落入池塘或湖泊的平静水面，会激起一圈圈向外扩展的波纹（图64）。
海浪拍打岸边，也能使大型船只剧烈起伏，航海故事中常有这样的描写。

水的溅拍声通过空气以声波的形式传到耳朵，而使我们看见物体的光也具有波动性质。
波动是自然界中十分普遍的现象。

不同波的产生原因各不相同，但正如不同的振动一样，许多波动现象可以用相同或相近的定量规律描述。
比较不同类型的波，有助于理解各自的运动规律。

什么是波？
波是怎样产生的？

固体、液体和气体中的质点相互作用。
当其中的质点开始振动时，这种相互作用使扰动以一定的速度向媒质中相邻的区域传播。

这种随时间在空间中传播的振动，叫作波。

空气、固体和液体内部的机械波，由联系媒质各部分的弹性作用传播。
水面波的恢复作用则来自重力和表面张力。

水面波能直观地说明波动的主要特点：圆形波峰逐圈向外传播，在近似规则的波列中，相邻波峰的间距大致相等。
一个轻小的漂浮物，例如火柴盒，通常不会跟随某个波峰一路向外移动，而会主要在原处附近上下起伏。

这里采用波幅较小、没有明显水流并忽略缓慢漂移的近似；
水的质点还可能有水平的往复运动，因此不能把这种观察理解为水只作严格的竖直运动。

波传播时，向外移动的是媒质的扰动状态，而不是同一批物质随着波形整体迁移。
石头使一处水面发生扰动，扰动传给相邻的水，再向周围扩展。

在前述忽略水流和漂移的近似下，水在平衡位置附近运动，向外传播的是水面的形状变化。
这不同于水流把水持续输送到远处。

波速是描述波动的重要特征。
波的传播并不是瞬时完成的，而是具有有限的速度。

设想一只海鸥沿波的传播方向飞行，始终跟随海面上的同一个波峰，那么它沿该方向的速度就等于这个波峰的传播速度。
水面波的传播通常不太快，因此比较容易直接观察。

横波与纵波可以用橡皮绳和弹簧来观察。
把橡皮绳的一端固定，轻轻拉紧，再使另一端振动，波就会沿绳传播（图65）。

对于同一根绳，在其他条件相近时，拉得越紧，波传播得越快。
波到达固定端后会反射回来。

传播的是绳的形状变化，绳的各段则在各自的平衡位置附近振动。
当各段的振动方向垂直于波的传播方向时（图66），这种波叫作横波。

并不是所有波都是横波。
如果媒质的振动沿着波的传播方向发生（图67），这种波叫作纵波。

用直径较大、较长而柔软的弹簧，可以方便地观察纵波。
用手掌拍一下弹簧的一端（图68a），被压缩的区域会作为一个弹性脉冲沿弹簧传播。

连续拍打可以产生相继传播的密部和疏部，形成纵波波列（图68b）。
弹簧的每一圈都沿着波的传播方向来回振动。

声波是尤其重要的一类机械波。
不过，研究声波比观察细绳或弹簧上的波更困难。

波的能量随着扰动从物体的一部分传到另一部分。
各类波共有的重要性质是传递能量，而不要求媒质物质随着波整体迁移。

使绳或弦振动的波源提供能量，能量随后随波传播。
橡皮绳中的机械能包括绳各段的动能，以及绳发生弹性形变时的势能。

波沿绳传播时，部分机械能会转化为内能。
这种能量损耗使振幅逐渐减小。

机械波需要气体、液体或固体这样的物质媒质。
电磁波则不需要物质媒质，无线电波和光都属于电磁波。

电磁场可以存在于没有原子等物质粒子的真空中，电磁波也可以在真空中传播。
因此，真空不意味着电磁场也不存在。

电磁波与机械波在物理机制上有本质区别，但两者都以有限的速度传播，并传递能量。
这些是不同类型的波共有的重要性质。

A stone falling into the still water of a pond or lake produces outward-spreading rings of ripples (Figure 64).
Sea waves break against the shore and can make even large ships pitch and roll, as many accounts of sea voyages describe.

The sound of splashing water reaches our ears as waves in the air, and the light that allows us to see objects also has wave properties.
Wave motion is widespread in nature.

Different kinds of waves have different physical causes, but, as with oscillations, many are described by the same or closely related quantitative laws.
Comparing different wave phenomena helps us understand how each behaves.

What is a wave?
How does a wave arise?

The particles in solids, liquids, and gases interact with one another.
When particles begin to oscillate, these interactions allow the disturbance to spread at a definite speed into neighboring regions of the medium.

An oscillation that spreads through space as time passes is called a wave.

Mechanical waves inside air, solids, and liquids propagate through elastic interactions that link neighboring parts of the medium.
For water-surface waves, gravity and surface tension provide the restoring effects.

Water waves illustrate the main features of wave motion: circular crests spread outward, and neighboring crests in an approximately regular wave train have roughly equal spacing.
A small, light floating object, such as a matchbox, normally does not travel outward with a particular crest but moves mainly up and down near its original position.

This description assumes small waves, no appreciable current, and negligible slow drift;
water particles can also move back and forth horizontally, so their motion is not strictly vertical.

As a wave propagates, the disturbance in the medium travels outward rather than the same body of matter moving along with the wave shape.
A stone disturbs one region of the water;
that disturbance passes to neighboring water and spreads into the surrounding regions.

In the approximation just described, with currents and drift neglected, the water moves near its equilibrium position while the change in surface shape travels outward.
This differs from a current that continuously carries water to a distant place.

Wave speed is an important characteristic of wave motion.
Propagation is not instantaneous: waves travel at finite speeds.

Imagine a seagull flying in the direction of propagation and continually keeping pace with the same crest on the sea;
its speed in that direction then equals the crest's propagation speed.
Water-surface waves usually travel slowly enough to be observed directly.

A rubber rope and a spring can be used to observe transverse and longitudinal waves.
Fix one end of the rope, pull it gently taut, and oscillate the other end;
a wave travels along the rope (Figure 65).

For the same rope under otherwise comparable conditions, greater tension produces a greater wave speed.
When the wave reaches the fixed end, it is reflected.

The changing shape travels along the rope, while each segment oscillates near its own equilibrium position.
A wave in which these oscillations are perpendicular to the direction of propagation is called a transverse wave (Figure 66).

Not every wave is transverse.
If the medium oscillates along the direction in which the wave propagates, the wave is longitudinal (Figure 67).

A long, flexible spring with a large coil diameter makes longitudinal waves easy to observe.
A tap with the palm at one end produces a compressed region that travels along the spring as an elastic pulse (Figure 68a).

Repeated taps produce successive compressions and rarefactions, forming a longitudinal wave train (Figure 68b).
Each coil of the spring oscillates back and forth along the direction of propagation.

Sound waves are a particularly important kind of mechanical wave.
Studying them, however, is more difficult than observing waves on a thin string or a spring.

A wave carries energy as its disturbance passes from one part of a body to another.
An important property shared by waves of every kind is energy transfer without requiring the matter of the medium to move along with the wave as a whole.

The source that sets a rope or string into oscillation supplies energy, which then travels with the wave.
In a rubber rope, the mechanical energy includes the kinetic energy of its segments and the potential energy stored in their elastic deformation.

As the wave travels along the rope, some mechanical energy is converted into internal energy.
This energy loss causes the amplitude to decrease gradually.

Mechanical waves require a material medium, such as a gas, liquid, or solid.
Electromagnetic waves do not require a material medium;
radio waves and light are examples.

An electromagnetic field can exist in a vacuum without atoms or other particles of matter, and electromagnetic waves can propagate there.
A vacuum therefore need not be free of electromagnetic fields.

Electromagnetic and mechanical waves differ fundamentally in their physical mechanisms, but both propagate at finite speeds and transfer energy.
These are important properties shared by different kinds of waves.
